howItWorks.intro: The math here follows a simple working assumption: pattern diameter opens up roughly in a straight line as shot travels downrange, and how fast it opens depends on how much the choke squeezed the column on the way out. An open Cylinder bore lets stragglers start peeling off within the first few yards, while a tight Improved Modified or Full choke holds the shot cushion together longer before it starts unraveling. That's a simplification of what's really happening — it ignores air drag on individual pellets, shot deformation inside the forcing cone, and wad separation — but it tracks closely enough with pattern-board results to be useful for choosing a choke before you load up for a hunt or a round of clays.

rules.name: Spread
rules.explanation: Tighter chokes have lower spread rates.

howItWorks.outro: Treat the spread and density numbers as a starting point, not gospel. Plastic versus fiber wads, buffered versus unbuffered loads, pellet hardness, and even barrel-to-barrel differences in forcing cone length will shift your real pattern by several inches in either direction — steel shot in particular tends to pattern noticeably tighter than lead through the same choke because the pellets don't deform on their way out. The only way to know exactly what your gun and load do at a given range is to shoot a pattern board, or a sheet of butcher paper stapled to a frame, and count holes inside a 30″ circle at your actual hunting or target distance.

faq.question: What choke should I use for what shooting?
faq.answer: Skeet and Improved Cylinder cover most shots inside 25 yards — think skeet stations, flushing quail, and grouse in tight cover. Modified is the general-purpose middle ground for pheasant, sporting clays, and most trap doubles out to roughly 35 yards. Improved Modified and Full are for longer, harder shots: pass-shooting waterfowl, rising trap singles past 40 yards, and turkey hunting, where a dense pattern in the head/neck zone matters more than overall spread.

faq.question: What's the effective range for a given choke?
faq.answer: There's no single number — effective range depends on pellet size, shot charge weight, and how many pellets you actually need in the target's vital zone, not just pattern diameter. As a rough guide, Improved Cylinder is usually solid to about 25-30 yards, Modified to about 35, and Full out to 40-45 yards with the right load. Past that, density drops off fast enough that a 'hit' can mean just one or two pellets connecting.

faq.question: Why does my real pattern look tighter or looser than the calculator says?
faq.answer: This model uses one fixed rate per choke, but a real pattern is shaped by your specific shell — wad design, pellet hardness, buffering, and forcing cone length all shift results. Steel shot patterns noticeably tighter than lead through the same choke because it doesn't deform going down the barrel. Use the calculator's number as a planning estimate, then confirm on a pattern board with your actual load.

faq.question: How is pattern density different from pattern spread?
faq.answer: Spread is just the diameter of the shot cloud — how wide it is. Density is how many pellets land inside a given area, usually judged against a standard 30″ circle. A choke can throw a wide pattern with weak density (too few pellets per square inch for a reliable multi-pellet hit) or a tight pattern with strong density. Spread tells you whether you'll cover the target at all; density tells you whether you'll hit it hard enough to cleanly connect.

faq.question: Is this a substitute for pattern-testing my gun?
faq.answer: No — it's a planning tool for narrowing down choke choice before you go to the range. Every gun-and-load combination patterns a little differently. The only way to know your real spread and density at a given distance is to shoot paper or a pattern board with the exact ammunition you plan to hunt or shoot with.

howWeCalculate.intro: Pattern spread comes from a single multiplier per choke: how many inches of diameter growth you pick up for every yard the shot travels. Below is the actual walkthrough, worked with real numbers, so you can see where the estimate comes from instead of trusting a black box.
steps: Start with the choke's rate factor — a stand-in for how quickly the shot column unravels. An open Cylinder bore (no constriction) opens fast, around 1.5″ of spread per yard. A Modified choke runs closer to 1.0″ per yard. A tighter Improved Modified holds the column together longer, closer to 0.85″ per yard.

Multiply the rate factor by distance in yards. Worked example: a 12-gauge with a Modified choke — roughly 0.020″ of constriction on a .729″ bore — fired at 30 yards, using a 1.0″/yard rate factor, gives 1.0 × 30 = 30″ of pattern diameter. That's almost exactly the standard 30″ circle used on a pattern board, which is no accident — Modified was historically tuned to print a usable pattern right around that distance.

Push the same gun out to 40 yards and the math scales linearly: 1.0 × 40 = 40″, well outside that 30″ reference circle. That's the practical reason Modified is generally treated as a 25-35 yard choke rather than a 40-plus-yard choke the way Full or Improved Modified are.

Density falls out of that same spread number. A 1 1/8 oz load of #6 shot holds roughly 250 pellets. At 30 yards with a 30″ pattern, those pellets are spread over about 707 square inches (π × 15²) — call it one pellet per 2.8 square inches. Stretch that same shot charge to a 40″ pattern at 40 yards (π × 20² ≈ 1,257 sq in) and you're down to roughly one pellet per 5 square inches. Same shell, same choke, noticeably thinner coverage — which is exactly the tradeoff every choke represents: how much area you cover versus how many pellets land in each square inch of it.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This is a planning estimate, not a substitute for a pattern board. Wad type, shot hardness, forcing cone length, and even barrel temperature all shift real pattern diameter and density. Pattern-test your actual hunting or target load through your actual barrel before you trust it on game, or under pressure on the line.

whenToUse.intro: Choke-versus-distance questions come up constantly around the gun cabinet and out in the field. Here's where this calculator actually earns its keep:
scenarios: Before a dove or upland hunt, deciding whether to stick with Improved Cylinder for close, fast flushes or step up to Modified for birds that tend to flush wilder as the season goes on
Setting up for a round of trap or sporting clays, where target distance is fixed by the course layout and choke choice is the one variable you can still adjust station to station
Comparing two choke tubes before buying — say the factory Modified against an aftermarket Improved Modified — to see if the extra constriction actually matters at your real hunting distance
Explaining to a new shooter why the same 12-gauge patterns completely differently at 20 yards over decoys versus 45 yards pass-shooting late-season ducks
Sanity-checking a choke recommendation from a buddy, a guide, or a forum thread against your actual shot distance instead of taking it on faith

sections.title: What Is the Shotgun Choke Pattern Calculator?
sections.body: Every choke tube is really just a controlled constriction — a short taper in the last few inches of barrel that squeezes the shot charge down before it clears the muzzle. Cylinder bore has essentially none of that squeeze; Full choke on a 12-gauge typically runs .035″-.040″ of constriction, tight enough to turn a pattern you'd normally see at 40 yards into something more like 25. This calculator takes the choke you've got mounted, or one you're considering, and the yardage you expect to shoot, and returns a working estimate of how wide the shot cloud opens and how dense it stays — the two numbers that actually decide whether a given choke is the right call for turkey, waterfowl, upland birds, or a round of sporting clays.

sections.title: Why This Calculation Matters
sections.body: Choke selection is one of the few variables a shooter still controls after the gun and shells are already bought, and getting it wrong shows up as misses that feel like bad luck but are really bad math. Run Full choke on close-flushing grouse in thick cover and you'll core the bird or miss clean because the pattern hasn't had room to open. Run Improved Cylinder on pass-shooting mallards at 45 yards and the pellets scatter too thin to reliably put two or three hits on a bird that size. The relationship between constriction, distance, and pattern density isn't something you eyeball accurately in the field — it's why pattern boards exist — but this calculator gives you the back-of-the-envelope version before you burn a box of shells confirming it on paper.

sections.title: When Should You Use This Calculator?
sections.body: Reach for this before you head to the pattern board, not instead of it. It's useful for narrowing down which choke tube is worth testing first for a specific hunt — say you're weighing Modified against Improved Modified for late-season pheasants flushing wild at 35-40 yards — or for understanding why a fixed Skeet or Cylinder barrel feels dead-on at 21 yards on station 4 but hopeless on longer true pairs. It also helps cut through choke-tube marketing: when a box claims extended range, the useful question is what constriction it's actually running and what that does to spread and density at the distance you actually shoot.

howToSteps.title: Select Your Choke
howToSteps.description: Choose the choke you're running or considering — Cylinder, Improved Cylinder, Modified, Improved Modified, or Full. If you're not sure what's threaded into your barrel, check the notch markings on the tube itself or measure bore constriction with a choke gauge.

howToSteps.title: Set Your Distance
howToSteps.description: Enter yardage in 5-yard steps from 5 to 60. Use your realistic shot distance for the game or target rather than the longest shot you could theoretically make — roughly 20-30 yards for most upland flushes, 35-45 for pass-shooting waterfowl, and 15-25 for skeet and closer trap presentations.

howToSteps.title: Hit Calculate
howToSteps.description: The calculator applies the selected choke's spread rate to your distance and returns an estimated pattern diameter and density instantly in your browser.

howToSteps.title: Read the Numbers Against Your Shot
howToSteps.description: Compare the pattern spread to the vital zone of your target — a dove's kill zone, a clay's face, a turkey's head and neck — and check whether the density estimate suggests enough pellets on target to cleanly connect at that range.

tips: Pattern-test with the actual shell you'll hunt with — steel, bismuth, and lead all pattern differently through the same choke, and steel especially tends to throw tighter than lead at equal constriction.

If you're torn between two chokes, bracket your real hunting distance rather than the longest shot you might theoretically take — most upland and waterfowl birds are killed inside 35 yards regardless of what the choke box promises.

A pattern that looks full on paper can still be too thin where it counts — count pellets inside the vital zone (roughly an 8″-10″ circle for most upland birds) rather than just eyeballing overall spread.
Screw-in chokes can loosen with recoil over a season of shooting — recheck tightness periodically and re-pattern after any tube swap, especially in an unfamiliar gun.

For turkey hunting, treat this calculator as a rough starting point only. Dedicated turkey chokes and TSS or heavy-shot loads often use constrictions well beyond .040″, and density in the head/neck zone matters far more than raw pattern diameter.
